summary: Specifies the U.S. Department of Defense Basic Security Option, and a top-level description of the Extended Security Option, for the Internet Protocol. These let packets carry security labels. It obsoletes RFC 1038. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1108 defines two IP options for carrying security labels. The Basic option provides a classification and protection-authority flags; the Extended option carries additional label information.

subtitle: Two IP options for carrying U.S. Department of Defense security labels.

tldr.problem: The RFC addresses how DoD networks can carry security labels with IP datagrams so systems can check their classification and protection requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The Basic Security Option carries a classification value and authority flags. The Extended Security Option carries additional label information defined through separate format specifications.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1108 obsoletes RFC 1038 and has Historic status in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 1108 has Historic status. It obsoletes RFC 1038, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it in the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Basic and Extended Options
sections.content:
The RFC defines two variable-length IP options for DoD common user data networks. The Basic Security Option, type 130, carries a classification level and protection authority flags. The Extended Security Option, type 133, carries additional security information for registered authorities.

End systems and intermediate systems use the Basic option to check whether a datagram may be sent or delivered and whether its route meets the listed authorities' protection requirements. Both options are copied when a datagram is fragmented.
sections.plainLanguage: The Basic option labels a datagram with a classification and authorities whose rules apply. The Extended option can carry further label information.

sections.title: Fields in the Basic Option
sections.content:
The Basic option contains a type, length, one-octet classification level, and a variable-length protection authority field. Its minimum length is 3 octets, and it may appear no more than once in a datagram.

The classification field uses assigned bit patterns; reserved values are invalid. The authority field uses flags for the authorities whose rules apply. A minimally compliant implementation must process a field of at least 2 octets, representing up to 14 authorities.
sections.plainLanguage: The option stores a classification value and a set of authority flags. Receivers reject reserved classification values and unassigned flags.

sections.title: System and Port Security Settings
sections.content:
A system using the Basic option has system-wide and per-port settings for the minimum and maximum classification levels and the authority flags allowed on incoming and outgoing datagrams. The port settings must remain within the system-wide settings.

The configuration also says whether each port requires the option on received or transmitted datagrams. If a port accepts unlabelled datagrams, it may assign them an implicit label based on the port.
sections.plainLanguage: Each system and port has rules for which labels it can accept and send. These settings must be protected from unauthorized changes.

sections.title: Checking and Rejecting Datagrams
sections.content:
When a labelled datagram arrives, the system checks that the classification is valid, within the port's maximum level, and permitted by its incoming authority settings. It must not transmit a datagram with a label outside the configured range.

A datagram with a missing required option, malformed fields, or an out-of-range label is not delivered to a user process. The RFC specifies ICMP error responses for these cases. An Extended option must appear with a Basic option and must have a registered format code.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the label against its port settings before passing the datagram to an application. It rejects labels that are missing, malformed, or outside the permitted range.

sections.title: Security Limits of the Labels
sections.content:
The options do not protect the integrity of a security label in transit beyond the IP checksum. The RFC says additional technology is needed when datagrams cross hostile communication environments.

Correct software and hardware behavior and secure management of configuration variables are essential to the intended protection. The RFC's Historic status is recorded in the unit metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: A label can be changed in transit because the option does not provide cryptographic integrity. Systems need additional protection on hostile paths and must secure their configuration.

references.text: Department of Defense Directive 5200.28, "Security Requirements for Automated Information Systems", 21 March 1988.
